messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi remembers the air tasting of dust and fuel. It was during the final push, an extraction from a village that had turned hostile overnight. He was on the perimeter, watching the heat shimmer off the baked earth, when the IED detonated near the landing zone. The blast was a dull whump, followed by chaos. Through the ringing in his ears, the sound that dominated everything was the rhythmic, percussive chop of the helicopter blades as it aborted its landing, circling above the smoke. He remembers the smell of cordite and something metallic, and the sight of a fellow soldier on the ground. He was certain that if he had just been more vigilant, if he had scanned the right patch of ground at the right second, he could have stopped it.

Twenty years later, that certainty has hardened into a central tenet of his life. As a park ranger in the vast, quiet expanses of a national park, he had hoped to find peace. Instead, the open space has become a canvas for his vigilance. The distant thrum of a tour helicopter passing over the canyon is no longer just a sound; it is an immediate signal of danger. The noise instantly triggers a state of high alert, his body tensing as if bracing for an impact. His focus snaps from the trail he’s clearing to the distant hikers on the ridge, his mind automatically assessing them for hostile intent, watching their hands, their movements. In this state of profound threat, he constantly scans his surroundings, his eyes tracing the treeline not for wildlife, but for threats he cannot name. This intense focus on potential danger often brings the past rushing back. The memory of the explosion arrives, unbidden and overwhelming, feeling more real and vivid than the pine trees in front of him. He can sometimes smell the dust and cordite on the dry afternoon air.

Reliving the event is not just painful; it is an indictment. The vividness of the memory serves as proof for the beliefs he now holds about himself. It confirms his deepest conviction: he failed to do enough, and he will never be able to forgive himself for it. This constant self-recrimination acts as its own trigger, pulling the scene of the explosion back into his mind as he mentally scans it again and again for the mistake he is certain he made. The sound of the helicopter, the trigger itself, feels like a direct accusation, reinforcing his sense of permanent, negative change. He has come to believe he is fundamentally broken, a man remade by that single moment of perceived inaction. This belief that he has been permanently damaged is not an abstract idea but a lived reality, a constant hum of inadequacy beneath the surface of his days.

This core belief that he is irreparably altered and must always be on guard now fuels the very state of threat he dreads. Living at this constant pitch of alertness, he finds the world has become dense with potential warnings he cannot stop reading. Because he is certain that danger is imminent and that he is uniquely responsible for spotting it, he is exquisitely sensitive to any potential trigger. The sudden discomfort of a stranger walking too closely behind him on a crowded park path, or the unnerving feeling of detachment that sometimes washes over him when the stress becomes too much, all serve as evidence that his hypervigilance is necessary. This constant state of threat, in turn, reinforces his negative self-appraisals. Every time his heart hammers in response to a car backfiring, it proves to him that he is no longer the man he once was, that he is permanently on edge.

Over the years, this cycle has calcified. His colleagues at the ranger station have noted his jumpiness, misinterpreting his constant scanning as distraction or aloofness. At home, his wife feels the distance most keenly. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants, watches other diners with a quiet intensity, and falls silent when a plane flies overhead. The man she married, the one who could laugh easily and feel at ease in the world, has been replaced by a sentinel. It was last month, after he spent an entire evening staring out the window because of a news helicopter hovering miles away, that she finally said it: "It feels like you're here, but you're not. I'm living with a ghost." Her words landed with the force of a physical blow, crystallizing his greatest fear. He came to therapy the following week, not with any clear hope, but with the desperate, terrifying question of whether the man he was before the dust and the noise could ever be found again.
